passage:
In the corridor outside the Class 5 room, parent-teacher day was busy. Payal, Ujjwal's mother, had just seen the maths paper. "Thirty out of a hundred?" she said loudly, in front of the other parents. "After all the tuition? Do you know what I gave up?"
Ujjwal, ten, stood very still, eyes on the tiles, and did not answer. The class teacher saw from the door and quietly came over. "Mrs Payal, may we sit in the library for a moment?"
Later that evening, at home, Payal sat on Ujjwal's bed. "I'm sorry I raised my voice. Can we look at the paper together?" Ujjwal nodded and pointed to the third sum.

qa.q: How many marks did Payal say Ujjwal had got?
qa.a: Payal said Ujjwal got thirty out of a hundred.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling while standing very still with eyes on the tiles?
qa.a: Ujjwal was frozen with fear and shame, unable to answer. Staring at the tiles shows a wish to disappear from the shouting.

qa.q: What made the conversation at home work better than the one in the corridor?
qa.a: At home Payal was calm, apologised for raising her voice and offered to look at the paper together. Ujjwal could listen and point to the third sum.

qa.q: How might the class teacher have seen the shouting in the corridor?
qa.a: The class teacher probably saw a frightened child and a stressed parent, and asked to talk in the library. Moving them out of the public corridor gave both space to calm down.

grounding: A child freezes while a mother shouts about marks in a school corridor, and only the later calm conversation lets the lesson land.

passage:
I live on the first floor across from Manjula's family, and I saw the whole thing from my balcony on Saturday. Manjula's father was shouting from the doorway about a cracked window. Manjula, nine, sat on the steps with the school bag hugged to her chest. At first she said, "It wasn't me, it was the ball!" and then, when the voice rose, she said nothing and folded smaller.
An hour later I saw them both on the steps with a mango cut in slices. He spoke softly and she nodded, once or twice. I can't say what was said, but she leaned on his arm.
— Sachin, neighbour

qa.q: What was the father shouting about?
qa.a: Manjula's father was shouting about a cracked window.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling as she folded smaller and said nothing?
qa.a: Manjula seems to have been scared and shut down as the voice rose. Sachin cannot know for sure, but hugging the bag and going quiet suggest fear.

qa.q: What did Manjula's father do later that could help the lesson land?
qa.a: He sat with Manjula on the steps an hour later, with a mango cut in slices, and spoke softly. A calm moment gave space for the talk.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Manjula's father to speak softly an hour later?
qa.a: He may have needed time to cool down himself, since the shouting had passed. Speaking softly suggests he wanted Manjula to hear him.

grounding: A child hearing a father shout freezes and shrinks, and a later calm conversation is when the lesson can land, as seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday. Raghav dropped his mother's phone and the screen cracked. Simran shouted, "How many times have I told you? Do you know what that costs?" Raghav froze. His mind went blank. He couldn't hear any words after the first shout, only the loudness.
Tuesday. After dinner, Simran sat beside him. She spoke quietly. "I'm sorry I shouted. I was angry and tired. Can we talk about the phone now?"
Raghav nodded, still wary.
"The phone isn't a toy because it's how Nani calls me from the village. Now it's harder to see her messages."
"I didn't know that," Raghav said. "I'm sorry, Mumma. Can I tape it?"
Saturday. Raghav's cousin reached for the new phone. Raghav said, "Careful, it's how Nani calls."

qa.q: What happened to the phone on Monday?
qa.a: The screen cracked when Raghav dropped it.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when Simran shouted?
qa.a: Raghav was frightened and froze, his mind going blank so he couldn't take in her words.

qa.q: Why did Tuesday's talk work when Monday's shouting did not?
qa.a: On Tuesday Simran was calm, apologised and explained why the phone mattered, so Raghav could listen and understand.

qa.q: How did Simran likely feel on Tuesday?
qa.a: Simran likely felt regretful about shouting and wanted to reconnect with Raghav.

grounding: A child freezes when a parent shouts, and the lesson lands only in a calm conversation later.

passage:
"Ishita, you look scared when your Papa raises his voice. Let your Tanuja Bua tell you what happened to me.
"When I was nine, I broke your Dadaji's reading glasses while playing cricket in the verandah. He shouted so loudly the neighbours looked over. I stood there, shrinking, and I remember only one thing: his voice. Not a single word.
"That night I couldn't sleep.
"The next morning he called me to the verandah and sat me on the swing beside him. He wasn't loud anymore. He said, 'Tanu, those glasses were my father's. That's why I got so angry. I'm sorry I shouted.' Then he told me stories about his father for an hour.
"I've never forgotten that. The shouting taught me nothing. The swing taught me everything.

qa.q: What did young Tanuja break?
qa.a: She broke Dadaji's reading glasses while playing cricket in the verandah.

qa.q: What was young Tanuja feeling while her father shouted?
qa.a: Young Tanuja felt frightened and small, shrinking so much that she heard only his voice and not a single word.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the lesson land, and why?
qa.a: The next morning her father sat her beside him on the swing, calmly explained why the glasses mattered and apologised, so she could finally understand.

qa.q: How did Dadaji likely feel the next morning?
qa.a: Dadaji likely felt sorry for frightening his daughter and wanted her to understand what the glasses meant to him.

grounding: An elder recalls freezing when a parent shouted, and learning only from the calm talk that came the next day.

passage:
They were already late for the wedding, stuck in Bengaluru traffic, when Ganga's mango juice spilled all over the new car seat.
Her father, Hrithik, shouted, "Can't you be careful even once? Look at this mess!"
Ganga shouted back, "It wasn't my fault! You braked!" Her face was hot, her heart thumping. She wasn't listening; she was defending.
The car went silent except for the horns.
At the wedding hall, after the ceremony, Hrithik found her on the steps with a plate of sweets. He sat down. "I shouted because I was stressed about being late. Not really about you."
"You did brake hard," Ganga muttered.
"I did. And the juice should have had its lid on. Both things are true."
Ganga thought. "Next time I'll close it. And you don't shout?"
"Deal."

qa.q: Where did Hrithik find Ganga after the ceremony?
qa.a: He found her on the steps with a plate of sweets.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she shouted back in the car?
qa.a: Ganga felt scared and defensive, her face hot and heart thumping, too busy protecting herself to listen.

qa.q: Why did the talk on the steps work better?
qa.a: Both were calm, Hrithik owned his stress and his braking, and Ganga could then see her own part and agree to close the lid.

qa.q: What would change if Hrithik had kept shouting at the wedding?
qa.a: Ganga would likely stay defensive and upset, and neither of them would learn anything from the spill.

grounding: A child argues back when a parent shouts, and the lesson lands only in a calm conversation later.

passage: In the Aizawl flat, the milk pan boiled over while Lalremsiami watched a cartoon, and the gas flame hissed out. Her mother, Reena, rushed in, turned off the knob and shouted, "How many times have I told you! Do you want to burn the house down?" Lalremsiami froze on the sofa, shoulders up to her ears. She nodded at everything and remembered nothing. That night Reena sat on her bed. "I shouted because I got scared. I'm sorry for the loudness. Can I show you what worried me?" In the kitchen she showed how spilt milk can put the flame out, and that a gas smell means knob off and window open. Lalremsiami repeated it back, then asked why gas smells at all. They looked it up together.

qa.q: What boiled over while Lalremsiami watched a cartoon?
qa.a: The milk pan boiled over.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami remember nothing of what was shouted?
qa.a: She was frightened by the loud voice, and the fear shut out the words, so she only nodded.

qa.q: Why did the evening talk work better than the shouting?
qa.a: Calm again, Reena apologised, explained her worry and showed the steps, so Lalremsiami could listen, repeat it back and even ask a question.

qa.q: What made Reena shout in the kitchen?
qa.a: Reena got scared when the flame went out, and her fear came out as shouting.

grounding: Shows a child freezing when a parent shouts and taking in nothing, and learning the lesson in a calm talk later that night.
